item.title: Population-based Prevalence of Bronchiectasis in the United States
item.description:
Background: Bronchiectasis is a chronic, heterogeneous lung disease of rising prevalence; however, contemporary epidemiological data are lacking. Furthermore, paediatric prevalence and cystic fibrosis (CF)-related bronchiectasis prevalence are frequently absent from existing literature.

Research question: What is the prevalence of bronchiectasis in the United States?

Study design and methods: This retrospective, observational study utilised data from the Optum® Clinformatics® Data Mart claims database to estimate the age- and sex-standardised prevalence of bronchiectasis in the US in people of all ages and paediatrics (aged <18 years). Prevalence was stratified by age, sex, ethnicity and insurance coverage. Individuals were required to have ≥1 day of enrolment during the index period (2018-2022); the index date was the latest day in this period with ≥365 days of prior continuous enrolment.

Results: In the overall population, 94,392 cases of bronchiectasis were identified (median age, 76 years). Five-year prevalence was 221.6 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 220.1-223.1) per 100,000 persons and increased with age. Prevalence was higher among females (274.6 per 100,000 persons), Asians (302.3 per 100,000 persons) and Medicare Advantage enrolees (528.6 per 100,000 persons). In total, 1.4% of the overall population had a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis. Five-year prevalence in the paediatric population (including 465 cases; median age, 12 years) was 11.9 (95% CI: 10.8-13.1) per 100,000 persons. Paediatric prevalence was similar between sexes, higher in Caucasians and higher in those with non-CF-related bronchiectasis than CF-related bronchiectasis.

Interpretation: This current study reports that bronchiectasis prevalence continues to increase in the US compared with previous studies, with a consistently higher prevalence in females and Asians, and that a lower proportion of individuals have CF-related bronchiectasis compared with non-CF-related bronchiectasis.

item.title: Subspecialty ILD Clinic Care is Associated with More Guideline-Concordant Evaluation and Improved Outcomes Compared to Other Ambulatory Settings: A Retrospective Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: Subspecialty interstitial lung disease (ILD) clinics are associated with improved outcomes, yet access remains uneven. Even within tertiary health systems, patients with ILD are managed across diverse ambulatory settings, with unclear implications for care and outcomes.

Research question: Within a single academic health system, do patient characteristics, care delivery, and outcomes differ between individuals with ILD managed in a subspecialty ILD clinic versus other ambulatory settings?

Study design and methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with ILD at a large academic medical center. Identified patients were stratified by care in a subspecialty ILD clinic versus non-specialty setting. Demographic, diagnostic testing, treatment, health care utilization, and survival data were extracted from the electronic health record. Diagnostic and treatment measures were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression. Hospitalization, emergency department visit, and death were analyzed as time-to-event outcomes.

Results: Among 6,637 patients with ILD, 4,371 (66%) were seen in the subspecialty ILD clinic. The 2,266 patients (34%) managed in non-specialty settings were more likely to identify as Black or Latinx, reside in more socioeconomically deprived neighborhoods, and have an unspecified ILD diagnosis (all p < 0.001). In the peri-diagnostic period, ILD clinic care was associated with higher adjusted odds of chest CT imaging (OR 2.51, 2.07-3.05) and antifibrotic therapy (OR 1.54, 1.32-1.80), and lower odds of lung biopsy (OR 0.47, 0.32-0.68). ILD clinic care was associated with a lower adjusted hazards of all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.46, 0.42-0.51), emergency department visit (HR 0.68, 0.59-0.78), and death (HR 0.57, 0.45-0.72). P-value <0.001 for all.

Interpretation: Within a single health system, subspecialty ILD clinic care was associated with more guideline-concordant care and improved outcomes. Differences in access to subspecialty expertise may contribute to inequities in care delivery, underscoring the need for scalable strategies, referral optimization, telemedicine, and clinical decision support, to extend ILD expertise and improve outcomes.

item.title: Azithromycin Exposure and Incident Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Isolation in Bronchiectasis and COPD: A Nationwide Nested Case-Control Study
item.description:
Background: Azithromycin reduces exacerbations in chronic airway disease, but whether it alters the risk of nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) isolation is unresolved.

Research question: Is azithromycin exposure in the preceding year associated with incident respiratory NTM isolation in non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis and in COPD?

Study design and methods: Two nationwide register-based nested case-control analyses in Denmark. Case patients had a first positive respiratory culture for NTM; controls, alive and free of prior NTM isolation on the index date, were matched 1:20 on age, sex, and comorbidity index. The prespecified exposure was at least 3,000 mg of azithromycin with at least two prescriptions redeemed in the preceding 12 months, with a 3-month lag. Conditional logistic regression was adjusted for inhaled and oral corticosteroids. Exploratory analyses examined an active comparator at matched thresholds, recency, and outcome stringency.

Results: The analyses comprised 173 cases and 3,409 controls (bronchiectasis) and 365 and 7,300 (COPD). Under the prespecified definition, azithromycin was not associated with incident NTM isolation (bronchiectasis: OR, 1.31; 95% CI, 0.79-2.18; COPD: 1.29; 0.78-2.13). In COPD, the OR was 1.61 (1.14-2.28) for one or more prescriptions and 1.29 (0.78-2.13) for two or more. The COPD association was concentrated within 90 days of the index date (2.55; 1.73-3.76) and attenuated with microbiological stringency (definite isolates: 0.77; 0.27-2.20). Non-macrolide antibacterials were more strongly associated than azithromycin at every matched threshold in bronchiectasis (one or more prescriptions: 1.90 [1.36-2.65] vs 1.15 [0.75-1.75]), and at the two higher thresholds in COPD (two or more: 1.48 [1.17-1.86] vs 1.24 [0.75-2.05]).

Interpretation: Azithromycin was not associated with NTM isolation under the prespecified definition. Associations under broader definitions were not dose-dependent and clustered close to the index date, more consistent with indication-driven testing than a drug effect, although in COPD an association with any exposure persisted after accounting for other antibacterials.

item.title: Clinical Phenotypes and Prognostic Heterogeneity of Mild-to-Moderate Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Prospective Community-Based Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: The clinical phenotypes, prognosis, and heterogeneity of mild-to-moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have not been systematically evaluated.

Research question: Do different clinical phenotypes of mild-to-moderate COPD have different prognoses?

Study design and methods: We analysed the baseline and 3-year follow-up data of participants with mild-to-moderate COPD from a prospective community-based cohort study. Mild-to-moderate COPD was defined as a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) / forced vital capacity ratio of < 0.70 and FEV1 ≥ 50% of the predicted value. The clinical phenotypes included respiratory symptoms, exacerbation history, emphysema, air trapping, and airway remodelling. Respiratory health outcomes included exacerbations and lung function decline over the 3-year follow-up.

Results: Overall, 806 participants with mild-to-moderate COPD were included, of whom 712 (88%) completed the 3-year follow-up. Participants with mild-to-moderate COPD had more severe emphysema, air trapping, and airway remodelling; increased exacerbation risk; and faster annual FEV1 decline than those with preserved spirometry. The severity of airflow obstruction, respiratory symptoms, emphysema, and air trapping, as well as the eosinophilic phenotype, had low overlap in mild-to-moderate COPD. There was significant individual variation in the annual FEV1 decline rate and exacerbation incidence among participants with mild-to-moderate COPD. Emphysema and air trapping were associated with faster FEV1 decline and higher exacerbation risk. Respiratory symptoms and exacerbations in the previous year were associated with a higher acute exacerbation risk but not with faster lung function decline.

Interpretation: Mild-to-moderate COPD exhibited distinct clinical phenotypes with significant prognostic heterogeneity. Accurate phenotype identification is essential for targeted intervention, clinical precision management, and prognostic improvement.
